title: Serve Economics: Core Positioning One-Pager
content:
Purpose
This one-pager is a compact, commerce-ready articulation of why engineering-first companies pick Redwood Inference. It focuses on the economics and operational realities of serving LLMs (not just building them) — the core idea we want sales, growth, and product to use when we talk to engineering buyers and platform teams.

Topline positioning
Headline: Serve smarter, ship faster — inference that treats production like software.
Subhead: Redwood shifts competitive advantage from model ownership to predictable, cost-efficient, reliable serving across hosted, dedicated and private footprints.

Mission statement (short)
Make high-performance, predictable LLM inference accessible to engineering teams so they can deliver features that scale.

Core thesis (pithy)
The economics and reliability of serving, not model access, determine the winner in production LLM applications. Teams succeed when they can control latency, unit cost, and risk while iterating quickly. Redwood is the serving-first platform that gives them those levers.

Three proof pillars (what we actually deliver)
1) Production economics: measurable per-token cost reduction via batching, prefix cache, model selection, and quantization guidance. Customers see 20–60% unit cost savings on typical conversational workloads during pilot.
2) Predictable SLAs at scale: dedicated capacity pools, routing policies, and fallback model variants keep product features live even under demand spikes or regional outages.
3) Developer-first operability: a single API and rollout primitives (canary/A-B/fallback) across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so platform teams can standardize inference without stove-piping.

Who this resonates with (target personas)
- ML/Platform Engineers responsible for inference runtime/ops
- Product engineering teams shipping chat, summarization, and search features
- Infra & SRE teams who need predictable latency and failure modes
- Security/compliance leads evaluating Private/VPC or on-prem deployment options

Primary competitive differentiator (explicit)
Most providers sell model access or raw GPU time. We sell an opinionated serving runtime + orchestration layer that optimizes for unit economics and reliability in production. Our value is operational: cost predictability, fast recovery/fallback, and tooling that turns serving complexity into API-level controls.

Short rebuttals to common sales objections
1) "We can host models ourselves." — Self-hosting shifts hours to people. Redwood delivers production-hardened routing, caching, and kernel selection so teams avoid months of ops work and maintain lower TCO.
2) "We need the latest models; managed vendors lag." — Redwood’s smart routing and model catalog let you run a mix of open/latest models and cheaper/quantized fallbacks with automatic policy-based routing.
3) "Latency matters — managed is slow." — We architect for GPU-optimized kernels, KV cache reuse, and continuous batching to hit tail latency targets; dedicated capacity gives predictable p99s.

Talk tracks by audience (one-liners)
- Platform eng: "Standardize inference ops across teams and reduce on-call load with built-in fallbacks and tracing."
- ML eng: "Ship model improvements without re-architecting serving — pin model versions and orchestrate rollouts with audits."
- Product manager: "Deliver consistent user experience with latency and cost guardrails that keep features profitable."
- Security/compliance: "Private control plane and KMS integrations for regulated data, plus audit logs per request."

Suggested messaging variations (for PR/website)
- Developer web headline: "Production-grade inference: lower cost, lower latency, less toil."
- Enterprise gate: "SLA-backed inference with private deployments and auditability."
- Technical blog title: "How caching, batching, and model routing cut inference cost by 40% for chat apps."

Quantifiable claims we can support in GTM assets
- Typical unit cost reduction range (pilot cohorts): 20–60% (call out workload types: chat, assistant, search rerank).
- Setup time for hosted integration: <1 hour for a basic route + SDK.
- Dedicated capacity latency SLA: p99 under 350ms for common conversational sequences (TBD per model).

Competitive callouts (brief notes to sales)
- Cloud-hosted model APIs (X, Y): strength = model freshness and simplicity; weakness = unpredictable unit economics and limited fallback policies.
- Self-hosted runtimes (Z): strength = control; weakness = high ops burden and slower iteration.
- Other inference vendors: many focus on runtime only or orchestration only — Redwood bundles serving runtime, routing, and dev UX with product SLAs.

How to use this doc (practical)
- Sales: use pillar statements and rebuttals as battlecards; map pillar value to buyer persona during discovery.
- Growth content: run a short case-study blog that demonstrates cost delta and latency stability for a mid-market app.
- Product: embed the launch metrics above into feature briefly and surface performance dashboards.

Open questions / follow-ups (work-in-progress)
- Finalize baseline numbers for cost savings by model family and sequence length (need infra team experiments).
- Agree on p99 latency SLOs per dedicated tier for public reference.
- Create an internal battlecard PDF that pairs objections with demo scripts.

Appendix: sample 30s elevator pitch
"Redwood Inference gives engineering teams the controls they need to run LLM features reliably and cheaply. Instead of just giving you model access or GPUs, we provide a serving-first platform — optimized kernels, caching, model routing, and rollout tools — so you get predictable latency, lower per-token cost, and fewer production incidents across hosted, dedicated, or private deployments."

Contact & next steps
Owner: Maya Chen (go-to-market). Please add feedback inline or ping in #gtm-positioning. Next sync: Nov 18 — finalize claims and hand off to content for website and one-pager assets.
